<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 1280 720">
  <!-- White background -->
  <rect width="1280" height="720" fill="#FFFFFF"/>
  <!-- Top orange bar -->
  <rect x="0" y="0" width="1280" height="6" fill="#D97757"/>

  <!-- Page label -->
  <text x="60" y="50" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13" font-weight="500" fill="#D97757" letter-spacing="2">FINDING 2 — CONTEXT LENGTH SCALING</text>

  <!-- Page title -->
  <text x="60" y="88" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="28" font-weight="bold" fill="#1A1A2E">Extending Context from 2K to 16K Tokens Unlocks Higher Image Resolution</text>
  <rect x="60" y="98" width="900" height="2" fill="#D97757" fill-opacity="0.3" rx="1"/>

  <!-- Takeaway box -->
  <rect x="60" y="108" width="1160" height="36" fill="#4A90D9" fill-opacity="0.07" rx="6"/>
  <text x="80" y="131" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14" fill="#4A90D9" font-weight="bold">KEY INSIGHT: </text>
  <text x="170" y="131" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14" fill="#1A1A2E">Increasing context from 2K to 8K–16K tokens enables more image tiles, higher effective resolution, and better performance</text>

  <!-- ===== LEFT COLUMN: Strategy ===== -->
  <!-- Step 1: The Problem -->
  <rect x="60" y="162" width="6" height="88" fill="#EF4444" rx="3"/>
  <text x="80" y="182" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="16" font-weight="bold" fill="#1A1A2E">Standard short-context VLMs: 2K token limit</text>
  <text x="80" y="202" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14" fill="#64748B">With r=4 compression, each image tile produces ~64 visual tokens</text>
  <text x="80" y="220" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14" fill="#64748B">A 2K context handles only a few tiles → low effective resolution</text>
  <text x="80" y="240" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14" fill="#EF4444">Performance significantly limited at 2K context</text>

  <!-- Step 2: The Solution -->
  <rect x="60" y="268" width="6" height="88" fill="#10B981" rx="3"/>
  <text x="80" y="288" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="16" font-weight="bold" fill="#1A1A2E">RoPE base increased: 10K → 273K</text>
  <text x="80" y="308" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14" fill="#64748B">Rotary Position Embedding base scaled 27× to support long</text>
  <text x="80" y="326" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14" fill="#64748B">positional sequences without accuracy degradation</text>
  <text x="80" y="346" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14" fill="#10B981">Enables robust positional encoding up to 16K tokens</text>

  <!-- Step 3: Training Approach -->
  <rect x="60" y="374" width="6" height="88" fill="#4A90D9" rx="3"/>
  <text x="80" y="394" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="16" font-weight="bold" fill="#1A1A2E">Fine-tuned on mixed long/short-context data</text>
  <text x="80" y="414" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14" fill="#64748B">Training data includes both long-context (multi-tile images, video</text>
  <text x="80" y="432" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14" fill="#64748B">sequences) and short-context samples</text>
  <text x="80" y="452" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14" fill="#4A90D9">Maintains performance on both short and long-context tasks</text>

  <!-- Impact summary -->
  <rect x="60" y="478" width="600" height="80" fill="#10B981" fill-opacity="0.07" rx="10" stroke="#10B981" stroke-opacity="0.3" stroke-width="1"/>
  <text x="80" y="500" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14" font-weight="bold" fill="#10B981">PERFORMANCE IMPACT</text>
  <text x="80" y="522" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14" fill="#1A1A2E">Significant benchmark improvement: 2K → 8K/16K context extension</text>
  <text x="80" y="542" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14" fill="#64748B">Multi-image reasoning and video understanding benefit most</text>

  <!-- Context → tiles visualization -->
  <rect x="60" y="578" width="600" height="60" fill="#F8FAFC" rx="8" stroke="#E2E8F0" stroke-width="1"/>
  <text x="80" y="598" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13" font-weight="bold" fill="#64748B">Context budget (with r=4, ~64 tokens/tile)</text>
  <rect x="80" y="608" width="40" height="16" fill="#EF4444" fill-opacity="0.6" rx="3"/>
  <text x="126" y="620" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="12" fill="#EF4444">2K → ~31 tiles</text>
  <rect x="240" y="608" width="80" height="16" fill="#10B981" fill-opacity="0.6" rx="3"/>
  <text x="326" y="620" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="12" fill="#10B981">8K → ~125 tiles</text>
  <rect x="450" y="608" width="120" height="16" fill="#4A90D9" fill-opacity="0.6" rx="3"/>
  <text x="576" y="620" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="12" fill="#4A90D9">16K → ~250 tiles</text>

  <!-- ===== DIVIDER ===== -->
  <line x1="682" y1="158" x2="682" y2="648" stroke="#E2E8F0" stroke-width="1"/>

  <!-- ===== RIGHT COLUMN: Parameters table ===== -->

  <rect x="706" y="200" width="514" height="36" fill="#1A1A2E" rx="6"/>
  <text x="800" y="223" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13" font-weight="bold" fill="#FFFFFF" text-anchor="middle">Model</text>
  <text x="960" y="223" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13" font-weight="bold" fill="#FFFFFF" text-anchor="middle">Context</text>
  <text x="1140" y="223" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13" font-weight="bold" fill="#FFFFFF" text-anchor="middle">RoPE Base</text>

  <!-- Row: SmolVLM-256M -->
  <rect x="706" y="236" width="514" height="44" fill="#F8FAFC"/>
  <text x="800" y="262" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14" fill="#1A1A2E" text-anchor="middle">SmolVLM-256M</text>
  <rect x="886" y="246" width="148" height="24" fill="#10B981" fill-opacity="0.15" rx="4"/>
  <text x="960" y="263" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14" font-weight="bold" fill="#10B981" text-anchor="middle">8K tokens</text>
  <text x="1140" y="262" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14" fill="#4A90D9" text-anchor="middle">273K</text>

  <!-- Row: SmolVLM-500M -->
  <rect x="706" y="280" width="514" height="44" fill="#FFFFFF"/>
  <text x="800" y="306" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14" fill="#1A1A2E" text-anchor="middle">SmolVLM-500M</text>
  <rect x="886" y="290" width="148" height="24" fill="#10B981" fill-opacity="0.15" rx="4"/>
  <text x="960" y="307" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14" font-weight="bold" fill="#10B981" text-anchor="middle">8K tokens</text>
  <text x="1140" y="306" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14" fill="#4A90D9" text-anchor="middle">273K</text>

  <!-- Row: SmolVLM-2.2B (highlighted) -->
  <rect x="706" y="324" width="514" height="48" fill="#4A90D9" fill-opacity="0.07" rx="4" stroke="#4A90D9" stroke-opacity="0.3" stroke-width="1"/>
  <text x="800" y="345" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14" fill="#1A1A2E" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="bold">SmolVLM-2.2B</text>
  <text x="800" y="362" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="11" fill="#D97757" text-anchor="middle">flagship</text>
  <rect x="886" y="334" width="148" height="24" fill="#4A90D9" fill-opacity="0.2" rx="4"/>
  <text x="960" y="351" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14" font-weight="bold" fill="#4A90D9" text-anchor="middle">16K tokens</text>
  <text x="1140" y="351" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14" fill="#4A90D9" text-anchor="middle">273K</text>

  <!-- Baseline comparison -->
  <rect x="706" y="380" width="514" height="44" fill="#EF4444" fill-opacity="0.04"/>
  <text x="800" y="396" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13" fill="#64748B" text-anchor="middle">Baseline (all)</text>
  <text x="800" y="413" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="11" fill="#94A3B8" text-anchor="middle">before extension</text>
  <rect x="886" y="390" width="148" height="24" fill="#EF4444" fill-opacity="0.12" rx="4"/>
  <text x="960" y="407" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13" fill="#EF4444" text-anchor="middle">2K tokens</text>
  <text x="1140" y="401" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13" fill="#64748B" text-anchor="middle">10K</text>

  <line x1="706" y1="432" x2="1220" y2="432" stroke="#E2E8F0" stroke-width="1"/>

  <!-- RoPE explanation -->
  <text x="706" y="460" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14" font-weight="bold" fill="#1A1A2E">What is RoPE base scaling?</text>
  <text x="706" y="482" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13" fill="#64748B">Rotary Position Embeddings encode token positions. A higher base</text>
  <text x="706" y="500" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13" fill="#64748B">value (10K → 273K) allows accurate encoding of longer sequences</text>
  <text x="706" y="518" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13" fill="#64748B">without needing architectural changes to the model.</text>

  <!-- Why this matters for vision -->
  <rect x="706" y="536" width="514" height="88" fill="#4A90D9" fill-opacity="0.06" rx="8" stroke="#4A90D9" stroke-opacity="0.2" stroke-width="1"/>
  <text x="726" y="558" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14" font-weight="bold" fill="#4A90D9">WHY THIS MATTERS FOR VISION</text>
  <text x="726" y="578" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13" fill="#1A1A2E">More context tokens = more image tiles fit in a single forward pass</text>
  <text x="726" y="598" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13" fill="#64748B">Higher-resolution images, multi-image QA, and video frames all benefit</text>
  <text x="726" y="616" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13" fill="#64748B">directly from expanded context without additional architectural overhead</text>

  <!-- Source note -->
  <text x="60" y="700" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="11" fill="#94A3B8">Source: SmolVLM (arXiv:2504.05299) — Finding 2: Extended Context Length</text>
  <!-- Page number -->
  <text x="640" y="700" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13" fill="#64748B" text-anchor="middle">6 / 9</text>
</svg>

    <defs>
        <!-- 背景渐变 -->

            <stop offset="0%" style="stop-color:#1A1A2E"/>

            <stop offset="100%" style="stop-color:#0F0F1A"/>

    <!-- 渐变背景 -->

    <g stroke="#4A90D9" stroke-opacity="0.3" stroke-width="1" fill="none">
        <path d="M150,150 Q250,100 350,180"/>
        <path d="M350,180 Q420,250 380,320"/>
        <path d="M950,400 Q1050,350 1100,420"/>
        <path d="M1100,420 Q1150,500 1080,550"/>
    </g>
    
    <!-- 节点装饰 -->
    <g fill="#4A90D9" fill-opacity="0.5">

        <circle cx="380" cy="320" r="4"/>

        <circle cx="1080" cy="550" r="5"/>
    </g>

        THANK YOU
    </text>
    
    <!-- 主感谢语 -->
    <text x="640" y="310" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="52" font-weight="bold" fill="#FFFFFF">
        {{THANK_YOU}}

        {{CONTACT_NAME}}

    <text x="640" y="535" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14" fill="#FFFFFF" fill-opacity="0.7">
        {{CONTACT_EMAIL}}
    </text>
    <text x="640" y="560" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14" fill="#FFFFFF" fill-opacity="0.6">
        {{CONTACT_URL}}
    </text>

    <text x="1220" y="680" text-anchor="end" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14" fill="#64748B">
        {{COPYRIGHT}}
    </text>

  <!-- Title -->

  <!-- Orange divider -->
  <rect x="490" y="96" width="300" height="3" fill="url(#orangeGrad)" rx="1.5"/>

  <!-- ===== 5 PRINCIPLE CARDS (2 top + 3 bottom, using 2+3 layout) ===== -->

  <!-- Top row: 2 cards -->
  <!-- Card 1: Balance Encoder-LM Compute -->
  <rect x="60" y="114" width="560" height="142" fill="#FFFFFF" fill-opacity="0.05" rx="10" stroke="#D97757" stroke-opacity="0.3" stroke-width="1"/>

  <text x="80" y="168" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13" fill="#FFFFFF" fill-opacity="0.8">Match vision encoder size to LM capacity. 93M SigLIP-B/16</text>
  <text x="80" y="186" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13" fill="#FFFFFF" fill-opacity="0.8">outperforms 428M SigLIP-SO400M for models ≤500M params.</text>
  <text x="80" y="204" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13" fill="#D97757">Bigger encoder ≠ better accuracy at small LM scale</text>

  <!-- Card 2: Extend Context Length -->
  <rect x="660" y="114" width="560" height="142" fill="#FFFFFF" fill-opacity="0.05" rx="10" stroke="#4A90D9" stroke-opacity="0.3" stroke-width="1"/>

  <circle cx="692" cy="145" r="16" fill="#4A90D9" fill-opacity="0.2"/>

  <text x="680" y="168" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13" fill="#FFFFFF" fill-opacity="0.8">Push RoPE base to 273K; extend context from 2K to 8K–16K</text>

arguments.content:
# 01_cover

SmolVLM is a family of compact vision-language models from Hugging Face and Stanford University, designed to bring competitive multimodal AI to edge devices. This presentation examines the three architectural innovations that make sub-1GB inference possible.

Key points: ① Three model sizes: 256M, 500M, 2.2B ② All open-source, including mobile app ③ arXiv:2504.05299
Duration: 1 minute

---

# 02_problem_motivation

[Transition] Let's start with why this problem matters.

State-of-the-art vision-language models are impressive, but they require 20 to 80 GB of GPU memory — far beyond what any smartphone or edge device can offer. [Pause] Even the best open-source efficient model, Molmo-A1B-7B, still requires 27.7 GB. That's 34 times more RAM than SmolVLM-256M.

[Data] The challenge: achieve competitive multimodal performance within a sub-1 GB memory budget. SmolVLM-256M answers this with just 0.8 GB at batch size 1.

Key points: ① Cloud VLMs require 20–80 GB RAM ② Best OS baseline still needs 27.7 GB ③ Edge budget is 2–16 GB ④ SmolVLM-256M fits in 0.8 GB
Duration: 2 minutes

---

# 03_architecture_overview

[Transition] So how does SmolVLM fit a competitive VLM into such a small footprint? The answer is a carefully designed five-stage pipeline.

Images are split into tiles, each encoded by a compact SigLIP vision encoder. The encoded features are then compressed via pixel shuffle — a space-to-depth operation — before being projected into the SmolLM2 language model's embedding space. Text and visual tokens are concatenated, and the language model generates the response. For video, frames are sampled and processed identically.

Three architectural findings drive every design choice in this pipeline, which we'll cover in the next three slides.

Key points: ① 5-stage pipeline: split → encode → compress → project → generate ② Same pipeline for images and video ③ Three findings: encoder size, context length, token compression
Duration: 2 minutes

---

# 04_compute_allocation

[Transition] The first finding challenges a common assumption: bigger vision encoder means better performance.

For compact VLMs, the opposite is often true. [Data] A 93M parameter SigLIP-B/16 encoder, paired with a 135M language model, outperforms the 428M SigLIP-SO400M paired with the same LM. Only at 1.7B LM scale does the larger encoder justify its 10% parameter overhead. [Pause]

This matters enormously for model design: SmolVLM's 256M and 500M variants use the 93M encoder, delivering 4.6 times fewer vision encoder parameters with better accuracy at that scale.

Key points: ① 93M encoder beats 428M for small LMs ② Large encoder justified only at ≥1.7B LM scale ③ SmolVLM 256M/500M use SigLIP-B/16
Duration: 2 minutes

---

# 05_token_compression

[Transition] The second architectural lever is token compression via pixel shuffle.

Pixel shuffle — also called space-to-depth — rearranges spatial features into the channel dimension. A shuffle factor of r reduces the number of visual tokens by r squared. [Data] At r=4, that's a 16× reduction: 64 tokens become just 4, while channel depth expands 16×. [Pause]

For small models where attention cost is the bottleneck, this is transformative. Fewer tokens mean each image fits comfortably within the 8K or 16K context budget. Larger models can afford r=2 — a 4× reduction — to retain more spatial detail for complex tasks.

Key points: ① r=4 → 16× fewer tokens ② Small models (≤500M): r=4; Large models (≥1.7B): r=2 ③ Reduces attention overhead critical for on-device inference
Duration: 2 minutes

---

# 06_context_length_scaling

[Transition] The third finding addresses a fundamental constraint: context length.

Standard VLMs operate with 2K token context windows, which severely limits how many image tiles they can process. SmolVLM extends this to 8K for the 256M and 500M variants, and 16K for the 2.2B model. The key technique is scaling the RoPE base from 10K to 273K — a 27× increase — which allows accurate positional encoding of much longer sequences without architectural changes.

The models are then fine-tuned on mixed long and short context data to maintain performance across both regimes.

Key points: ① Context extended 2K → 8K/16K ② RoPE base scaled 10K → 273K ③ More context = more tiles = higher effective resolution
Duration: 2 minutes

---

# 07_benchmark_performance

[Transition] Let's look at how these three architectural choices translate into real benchmark results.

SmolVLM was evaluated across 13 benchmarks spanning single-image understanding, multi-task reasoning, and video comprehension. [Data] SmolVLM-256M achieves 44.0% average — at just 0.8 GB RAM. SmolVLM-500M reaches 51.0% at 1.2 GB. And SmolVLM-2.2B achieves 59.8% at 4.9 GB — rivaling models that consume twice the memory. [Pause]

For comparison, Molmo-A1B-7B — the best open-source efficient baseline — requires 27.7 GB of RAM. SmolVLM-256M notably outperforms the 300× larger Idefics-80B, despite an 18-month development gap.

Key points: ① 256M: 44.0% avg, 0.8 GB ② 2.2B: 59.8% avg, 4.9 GB ③ Molmo-A1B requires 27.7 GB ④ SmolVLM-256M beats Idefics-80B
Duration: 3 minutes

---

# 08_on_device_deployment

[Transition] These aren't just paper results — SmolVLM runs in production on consumer hardware today.

The HuggingSnap iOS app processes photos and video entirely on-device, with no cloud dependency. [Data] On an M1 Max Pro 64GB, SmolVLM-256M achieves roughly 80 tokens per second at batch size 1. On a MacBook Air M3 with 16GB RAM, it still produces 55 tokens per second. And at batch size 64, throughput approaches 1,000 tokens per second on high-end devices. [Pause]

All weights, code, and the HuggingSnap app are publicly released to accelerate on-device AI research.

Key points: ① ~80 tok/s on M1 Max Pro (batch=1) ② ~55 tok/s on MacBook Air M3 ③ ~1000 tok/s at batch=64 ④ Full open-source release including mobile app
Duration: 2 minutes

---

# 09_key_takeaways

[Transition] Let me close with the five design principles that SmolVLM demonstrates for efficient multimodal models.

First, balance your encoder and language model compute — bigger encoders are wasteful at small LM scales. Second, extend context length aggressively using RoPE scaling. Third, compress tokens hard for small models — r=4 pixel shuffle gives 16× reduction with minimal accuracy loss. Fourth, sub-1GB inference is real and practical today. And fifth, open-source everything to accelerate the field.

[Pause] The central lesson: architectural efficiency, not raw scale, is the key to practical on-device AI. SmolVLM-256M proves this by outperforming a model 300 times its size.

Key points: ① Balance encoder-LM compute ② Extend context (2K → 16K) ③ Compress tokens aggressively (r=4) ④ Sub-1GB is achievable ⑤ Open-source accelerates research
Duration: 2 minutes

---

# 02_problem_motivation

[Transition] Let's start with why this problem matters.

State-of-the-art vision-language models are impressive, but they require 20 to 80 GB of GPU memory — far beyond what any smartphone or edge device can offer. [Pause] Even the best open-source efficient model, Molmo-A1B-7B, still requires 27.7 GB. That's 34 times more RAM than SmolVLM-256M.

[Data] The challenge: achieve competitive multimodal performance within a sub-1 GB memory budget. SmolVLM-256M answers this with just 0.8 GB at batch size 1.

Key points: ① Cloud VLMs require 20–80 GB RAM ② Best OS baseline still needs 27.7 GB ③ Edge budget is 2–16 GB ④ SmolVLM-256M fits in 0.8 GB
Duration: 2 minutes

---

# 03_architecture_overview

[Transition] So how does SmolVLM fit a competitive VLM into such a small footprint? The answer is a carefully designed five-stage pipeline.

Images are split into tiles, each encoded by a compact SigLIP vision encoder. The encoded features are then compressed via pixel shuffle — a space-to-depth operation — before being projected into the SmolLM2 language model's embedding space. Text and visual tokens are concatenated, and the language model generates the response. For video, frames are sampled and processed identically.

Three architectural findings drive every design choice in this pipeline, which we'll cover in the next three slides.

Key points: ① 5-stage pipeline: split → encode → compress → project → generate ② Same pipeline for images and video ③ Three findings: encoder size, context length, token compression
Duration: 2 minutes

---

# 04_compute_allocation

[Transition] The first finding challenges a common assumption: bigger vision encoder means better performance.

For compact VLMs, the opposite is often true. [Data] A 93M parameter SigLIP-B/16 encoder, paired with a 135M language model, outperforms the 428M SigLIP-SO400M paired with the same LM. Only at 1.7B LM scale does the larger encoder justify its 10% parameter overhead. [Pause]

This matters enormously for model design: SmolVLM's 256M and 500M variants use the 93M encoder, delivering 4.6 times fewer vision encoder parameters with better accuracy at that scale.

Key points: ① 93M encoder beats 428M for small LMs ② Large encoder justified only at ≥1.7B LM scale ③ SmolVLM 256M/500M use SigLIP-B/16
Duration: 2 minutes

---

# 05_token_compression

[Transition] The second architectural lever is token compression via pixel shuffle.

Pixel shuffle — also called space-to-depth — rearranges spatial features into the channel dimension. A shuffle factor of r reduces the number of visual tokens by r squared. [Data] At r=4, that's a 16× reduction: 64 tokens become just 4, while channel depth expands 16×. [Pause]

For small models where attention cost is the bottleneck, this is transformative. Fewer tokens mean each image fits comfortably within the 8K or 16K context budget. Larger models can afford r=2 — a 4× reduction — to retain more spatial detail for complex tasks.

[Transition] The third finding addresses a fundamental constraint: context length.

Standard VLMs operate with 2K token context windows, which severely limits how many image tiles they can process. SmolVLM extends this to 8K for the 256M and 500M variants, and 16K for the 2.2B model. The key technique is scaling the RoPE base from 10K to 273K — a 27× increase — which allows accurate positional encoding of much longer sequences without architectural changes.

The models are then fine-tuned on mixed long and short context data to maintain performance across both regimes.

Duration: 2 minutes

---

# 07_benchmark_performance

[Transition] Let's look at how these three architectural choices translate into real benchmark results.

SmolVLM was evaluated across 13 benchmarks spanning single-image understanding, multi-task reasoning, and video comprehension. [Data] SmolVLM-256M achieves 44.0% average — at just 0.8 GB RAM. SmolVLM-500M reaches 51.0% at 1.2 GB. And SmolVLM-2.2B achieves 59.8% at 4.9 GB — rivaling models that consume twice the memory. [Pause]

Key points: ① ~80 tok/s on M1 Max Pro (batch=1) ② ~55 tok/s on MacBook Air M3 ③ ~1000 tok/s at batch=64 ④ Full open-source release including mobile app

Duration: 2 minutes
